blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: I'm not going to go through all of them, but they include things like potential problems with breathing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: And as we've heard, and as I'm sure we'll hear in more detail, that's because in a premature baby, or very premature baby, the development of the lungs hasn't yet got to the stage that it would have done in a full term baby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: So they may struggle to breathe. There are problems with feeding preterm babies compared to a term baby, aren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: I don't think I could comment whether their veins are more or less robust.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: I just want to confirm one matter. I asked you yesterday about intensive care and I'm not going to go through every aspect of how it's categorised, but in fact whether or not a baby is in intensive care is also something that's defined by the BAPM guidelines, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: And can you help us with this? At the time we are talking about, in 2015, and if you can't we can deal with this another way, a baby fitted with a UVC would be considered an intensive care baby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: That's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: So certainly, by about 1 o'clock of the afternoon that you were there, [Baby A] had become an intensive care baby, hadn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Because, as I'll remind everyone, he'd been fitted with a UVC.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And also, is it right that a baby who was on CPAP and receiving parenteral nutrition was also considered intensive care?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That I'm not so sure. I would have to refer to the guidelines for that possibly.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: But in any event, during the course of that day, you certainly were in a position where you had at least one intensive care baby and one other baby that required a lot of care?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: That's correct, isn't it? And it was just you dealing with both of them at that point, in terms of nursing, wasn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Which is actually at a point below what the guidelines would say, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, repeat that again?
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: It's actually below what the guideline quota is, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. And in terms of ITU, you know, some of the BAPM guidelines, technically they are intensive care but they are not always as intensive care -- if it was a baby who was on a ventilator and needing lots and lots of support, they are very — they need a lot, a lot of care, they are very hands-on and one-to-one is definitely needed. Whereas a baby on CPAP who is stable -- some of the things they do technically become ITU but in terms of care they may be fairly similar to an HDU patient.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: So it may be, in real terms, possible to manage them, although it may fall outside the guidelines?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: But do you accept -- I won't ask you to comment on the guidelines, but we have them.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: During that day that shift had been very busy, hadn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: And indeed, do you agree the unit was extremely busy round about this time or so it felt?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Just so we can have an understanding, during the course of a day there, are there people moving about constantly across the nurseries and through the unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: And a lot of tasks to be done?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: And actually, is there quite a lot of background noise with alarms and monitors sounding around the place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There can be.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Was your impression that over this particular period, so let's say getting into early summer 2015, there did seem to be a lot of poorly babies and the unit was getting very busy indeed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I mean, to be honest, I remember that shift was a busy shift and I remember having a lot of busy shifts around that time. I can't comment sort of directly before, exactly around that time. But there were definitely busy shifts and that was a busy shift.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Yes. Did you get the impression that that coincided with an increase in the number of poorly babies or babies with higher acuity, to use a technical expression?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think inevitably if you've got a higher number of babies there will be a higher number of babies needing HDU/ITU care.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: That then puts an increasing demand, for example, on the nursing staff who are available to deal with them, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Amongst the duties you deal with, we have heard, are the observations that are taken regularly on the babies.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to put up, please, if we could, J1123, which, ladies and gentlemen, if you're using the timeline, is at slide 7. There are two ways of referring to them.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The exhibit number is J1123.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We'll try and match it to the screen. Perhaps just broaden it a little bit, if you could, please, Mr Murphy. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We're getting familiar with these, Miss Taylor. Can we scroll down, please, just to look at the temperature section? Just enlarge that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: When we look at the chart we'll see when we look at heart rate and respiration that on the hourly checks, invariably there is a mark put in for heart rate and respiration and we can see, looking at temperature, that every now and again it looks like there hasn't been a mark put in for temperature.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Can you see that? I'll just ask you why that is.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you help us why -- is there a reason why, for instance, you won't do temperature every hour in the way that you might do heart rate and respiration every hour?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. It is standard that we would not necessarily do temperature every hour. To do a temperature we have to put a probe underneath the baby's arms, they often don't like it, whereas respiratory rate and heart rate we don't need to do that. And you can see within the ones where I have not done them hourly, they've been within normal range, so if I'm happy with the temperature I won't check it hourly, whereas the ones that have gone into the yellow, I've checked it the next hour and it has been in a normal range, so I have again not done it for another hour.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: I am just going to go into that in a little more detail, but I'm grateful for that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You can tell what the heart rate or what the respiration are from the monitors that are fixed around the cot, can't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: To enter those you simply look at that and then mark it down on the chart. Taking the baby's temperature --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, I was just going to say: for respiratory rate we wouldn't read that off the monitor, we would count that ourselves.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: You'd count it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: It doesn't involve touching the baby though, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: And that's the point, isn't it, because to take the baby's temperature you have to handle the baby, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: And as a general rule, is handling kept to a minimum with neonates like this, so far as you can?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: It's something that people in neonatal nursing are familiar with, I'm going to suggest, that handling can become a direct source of stress for the little babies that you look after; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Is it the case some handling is regarded as what you might call positive handling?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Could you give an example of positive handling?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's positive touch, which is placing a hand or two hands on a baby, such as the stomach and the head, just for containment and making the baby feel secure. We call that positive touch. That can actually reduce heart rate and be positive, as well as skin-to-skin touch is also with the parents. So yes, that's positive touch.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: But even that in fact has to be controlled to some extent with a vulnerable neonate, doesn't it, the skin-to-skin contact with parents?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It depends on the baby and it depends on the situation.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: I think you would judge it on what condition the baby was in to decide that.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: Is it possible that handling that causes -- handling of a baby may cause an increase in stress which can actually lead to a deterioration in the baby's condition?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... To a certain degree, yes. Yes.
blocks.speaker: TAYLOR

blocks.text: So all of that lies behind why it is that, when temperature is already stable, you don't necessarily take another temperature reading?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: UVC is an umbilical venous catheter, so it's a tube that goes into the blood vessels of the umbilicus, the belly button. That's a nice thick tube that we can give fluids or medication or feed through. So that's what we tend to do to start with because it tends to be easier to put in. However, once it's gone through the umbilicus, it can either go up towards the heart, through the vena cava or it can veer off to the right and go off towards the liver instead, which is completely unavoidable, but we prefer it to be going into the IVC, the vena cava, which is the main blood vessel. So when we get an X-ray to look for the position, if it's not in the IVC, we tend to try and have something that is in a better position. However, what we can do otherwise is pull the line lower so it — before it would go in towards the liver and we can use it in what we call a low position. So we tend to only use that for the short-term to make sure we're giving fluids whilst we look for a long line, but it's a safe way that we will use things until we have something better in place.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So as on the previous page, that was the oxygen levels being 70 to 80% rather than the 90 per cents that I would like:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Heart rate on monitor 90-110."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So, again, as I have mentioned before, roughly speaking where you'd want it -- you'd want it over 100.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So when I've listened it's over 100 and I've put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Impression at the time: was this the second to long line? Long line removed 20.27. Help called at 20.27."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So at this point in time I wasn't sure -- the long line for me was one of the last things that I put in so I decided to think whether or not that was an issue so I removed it at that point in time to be certain and called for help.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I then intubated:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "First attempt size 3, 7cm at lips at 20.28."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So intubation is essentially where you put a tube that goes down into the windpipe and means that you've got a definitive way of giving oxygen into the lungs and inflating the lungs. So the Neopuff works quite well but it requires someone to hold it with two hands for a long time, so what you can do is when you ventilate a baby you can put the tube down and do that --
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there, Dr Harkness, I am just going to over it a little more slowly.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The monitor informed you as to the heart rate. You then listened in the traditional stethoscope way?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: That's auscultation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Once you get to 100 in a minute it's difficult to keep count --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- of so many beats in such a short time so you approximate that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I think it says "on auscultation".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: It's not "OI", your writing's just been misread.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's just bad doctor's handwriting.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Is what you have just told us, because this event was relatively soon after the introduction of the long line, training, experience, caused you to question whether the long line was indeed the cause --
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So that was my immediate thought. Again, in hindsight, looking through things, there was no possible way that there was a link. Again, in my statement I explain it more, but essentially where it sat is a safe place for it to sit. If it has a wire running through it, which is what we use when we put it in, the wire, if left long enough, can poke a hole into the heart. The wire was gone and there was no chance that could happen and the post-mortem confirmed that hadn't happened.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: When it comes to the other risks that can happen, that's if it goes all the way into the heart, which we know it didn't, then it can tickle the pacemaker of the heart and make your heart goes faster. If that had happened, his heart rate would have been over 200 as opposed to 100.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So for me at the time this was a knee-jerk reaction because in my mind this is the last thing that has changed and therefore should be the first thing to go, but there was no actual evidence since at the time or since that has supported that being any cause.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Within the crisis of the moment --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- you wished to eliminate a potential cause?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Help called at 20.27."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Expand upon that for the jury.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That would have been a neonatal arrest call. Typically we were all there anyway, so that would be nurses doctors and it would also go through to my consultant.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So in hours that will go to a consultant bleep system, out of hours it will be a phone call to the consultant on call to come and help us.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Also it would have been the immediate area as well if we needed more nursing staff, more nursing staff would come.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby A] was intubated at the first attempt by you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's obvious to you, but just remind us why there was an urgent need to intubate the baby in these circumstances?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: With these pauses in breathing that weren't changing — as I've mentioned with the Neopuff, there's only so long that someone can sit there and breathe for him, so by putting him on to the ventilator we can do all the breathing for him and leave him be for some rest, so it's the safest and most secure way to make sure we can support him with his breathing long term. And at this point in time was the ideal point to do it because at this point he was otherwise stable, his observations were fine, and so it was the perfect opportunity. Where things were as under control as they could be for a baby that's having these pauses in breathing, it was the ideal time to do it.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So it was a successful intubation at the first attempt, the note tells us, it then tells us the size of the tube used.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Which is selected to be appropriate (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. We select the size of the tube and how far it needs to go in based on either how much they weigh or by gestation of the baby, so how many weeks old they are.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So that will give us an idea of how big and how far to do it.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I've also put then:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Visualised passing cords."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So to ensure you're going into the right place you look at the vocal cords and if you can see that the tube goes clearly through the vocal cords you know you have gone into the right place. The risk is if you haven't seen it, it could have gone into the stomach instead and you're not helping inflate the lungs. That's why we comment on that one.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So size of tube, 3. How far, 7 centimetres.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And that's at the lips, so all the measurements are from the baby's lips.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And you would have estimated 7 centimetres was the desired --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And you don't merely rely on measurement, you actually looked, checked (overspeaking) right place?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We look to make sure it's in right place and then what you would do afterwards, if the baby was stable, would be to get a chest X-ray and that will tell you it's exactly -- the exact position. Obviously in this case this wasn't appropriate at that point in time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You said you would look to see the exact position of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Of the tube, where that is in relation to the windpipe, and that would be based on the X-ray. And you will know by the fact that the chest is moving and the oxygen levels have come up that you're in the right place. The risk with a tube is, if it's too low, it can slip further down and only inflate one lung. If it's too high there's a risk it could be pulled out. So although you know it's in the lungs and in the windpipe you sometimes want to make some finer adjustments to make sure it's in the perfect position. But we were completely happy that it was doing what it needed to do at that point in time and working as it needed too.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You have recorded, relying on Dr Wood's contemporaneous chronology, that that event took place at 20.28; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Next line:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "HR dropped to 60-70 at 20.28."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's his heart rate that's dropped. So our heart rate, we like it to be over 100. We are very concerned if it drops below 60. Below 60 you start to do CPR and you start to do chest compressions. So that was a deterioration that had started to happen after that point in time. So then what I've written is:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Chest compressions started at 20.28 [as well]."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So the heart rate has dropped to round about the 60 mark, this is where we're not happy, this is where we started to do the chest compressions. Different to adults because obviously children are a lot smaller but you're pushing on the chest to try and help push the blood around the body and get the heart started again.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Then we've given 10ml per kilo of normal saline. So we give salt water as an injection and what happens is that salt water helps to push that blood a bit further round the heart and it means there's more fluid there to be pumped around so that's one of the first things that we tend to do.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We've also then at 20.23 given adrenaline, so adrenaline makes the heart pump. So what we try and do is do the chest compressions to help push the blood and you give the medications to try and help it to pump as well. So between the two ideally it starts the heart back pumping again.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: It may have been a slip of the tongue there. Saline given at 20.31 and the adrenaline given at 20.33. You said 23.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: It was a slip of the tongue. It was obviously a slip of the tongue.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Unless you can remember it was 10 minutes earlier than shown!
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So then it's recorded that Dr Ravi Jayaram, who was the on-call consultant, is that right?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Arrived at the incubator side at 20.33.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Patient reviewed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Patient reviewed with Dr Jayaram, yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: What about the next entries are they --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the UVC that I've alluded to before was still in the place and, like I initially mentioned, is that -- if we are not in the ideal position in the vena cava we pull it back to a lower position and new use -- so the decision between myself and Dr Jayaram was that that would be what we would do because we didn't have that long line in place, so the best thing to do was to pull that back and start to use that --
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there. That takes us where we started really, doesn't it? There was always a UVC in place?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: It was fit to be used in the short term. You decided it would have been -- a long line would be preferable, so you inserted the long line, but when this collapse happened, just in case, you removed --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- the long line? So that is back to plan A, as it were --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- and the (overspeaking) UVC?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which is exactly why. It's that kind of eventuality that means that you want to keep something in place.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Next line.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So we then summarised what was happening at the time, so:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Continued good chest movement and air entry."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So what I'm saying there is that he's being ventilated now with the tube into his windpipe and the chest is still moving, and I can hear the air going into his lung with the stethoscope, so know that the air is getting into the lungs and everything between the ventilator and the lungs is working as it should be.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We then listen in for the heart rate. At this point, unfortunately, when I'm listening with my stethoscope there's no heart rate at all.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I've put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Electrical activity noted on monitor, small complexes."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So what happens is even when your heart stops the ECG, which is the kind of wiggly line you see at the beginning of Casualty and hospital programmes, will still show potentially what looks like your heart is still working, but that can still happen despite your heart not beating.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So there are other types of problems that you can get when your heart stops that will show you different patterns, so this was just commenting on that pattern at that time. But essentially his heart at this point has stopped and isn't pumping at all.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there: so notwithstanding the markers on the monitor, you would rely upon the stethoscope, the information --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- received down the stethoscope?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So what I can hear and what I can see with baby — we would also check the pulses in the groin. That will trump what the monitor is showing me at that point in time. But it's useful to know and record both.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So CPR was continued?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. We carried on giving the chest compressions and carried on giving the breathing with ventilation.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I then essentially have listed the other -- what we do is we'll give the adrenaline, we will check for the heart rate. If it's not there, we'll carry on giving chest compressions. We then give another dose of adrenaline, check for the heart rate, and carry on.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: This is -- what I've then documented is the various medications being given and being checked over the space of the next 10 to 15 minutes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. So second adrenaline given at 20.35. Sadly, still no heart rate detected? Third given at 20.37.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again, sadly, no heart rate detected. And then next line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Second -- that's a bolus of 0.9 saline, so salt water that we have given before. Still no heart rate heard.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Fourth dose of adrenaline given at 20.41 and again still no heart rate. So we're not making any difference, unfortunately, at this point this time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We have then moved on to give sodium bicarbonate, which helps with acid that builds up in the blood. If you have got acids in your blood, which is part of being very tired out, this can help get rid of some of those acids and can help the heart as well. Se we have given that at 20.43 and still no change.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And then we've given a further dose of adrenaline at 20.45 and we've gone on and on at this point.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Then we've given some sugar at 20.48. If your blood sugar is very low it can cause you to -- your heart to stop beating so we have given some sugar as well. We have given more adrenaline at 20.49.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We then noticed a heart rate at 20.50. So we've heard a slight heart rate -- again 60 is where we would start the chest compressions below, so we have heard it, but because it's still less than 60, we've carried on giving the chest compressions and the CPR in the next review at 20.57.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Unfortunately, at 20.57, Dr Jayaram has then reviewed and we have not had a heart rate again and we stopped resuscitation at 20.58.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So, sadly, when you're going on for this period of time, even though you hear a heart rate, the heart rate was never high enough that he would have lived and had enough blood going round his body to survive. So at this point it was felt the kindest thing to do was to stop resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you, doctor. Could you confirm that the process that you've just taken us through minute by minute is the prescribed --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- response to these circumstances?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. This follows a national APLS, which is a Resus Council national guideline that everywhere in the UK will follow. That's a neonatal life support guideline which everywhere in the UK will follow the same guideline, so it's standardised care.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We've focused in detail on the minute-by-minute events as recorded by you, with the assistance of Dr Wood, but taking a step back from the note and going back to the incubator side, is there anything you want to inform the jury about how [Baby A] presented when you went to the incubator and when you did all you could to save him?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was incredibly unexpected. This was a completely stable, well baby who had no reason to suddenly deteriorate, so I was very surprised to be called back and to need to do any of this at the time. Something that I've documented later on as well is there was very unusual patchiness of his skin, which I'd never seen before, and I have only seen in cases since within the Countess of Chester and nothing other than that.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So that was -- I was faced with a baby that was unexpectedly deteriorating with no clear reason and a baby that had an unusual skin colour and skin change, which again I'd never seen. So it was a very unusual and unexpected situation.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there, you've referred to this unusual skin colour or discolour. Could you describe it? Can you remember it? Could you describe it in detail to the jury?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So it was very -- I've only ever seen it in [Baby A] and I can only recollect one other baby that's part of the trial.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there, can you remember the name of that baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. It was one of the [Surname of Babies E & F] twins.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll come back to that. Let's keep our focus on [Baby A]'s discolouration. Can you describe it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There were patches of kind of blue/purple colour, there were patches of bright red colour, there were white patches, and they didn't fit with something that you would find on a baby that's not pumping any blood around their body. That can look purple and can be pale, but it doesn't look anything like this patchy pattern that this baby had. It's very difficult to describe other than that. Ideally, you would want a photo of it -- because, as I said, I've never seen it before or since -to have a comparison.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Was it constant?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was there from shortly after the event started and then -- it -- it wasn't constant in the fact that as he then
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: deteriorated and stopped, his heart stopped beating, he then went pale and purple, which is what you'd expect from a baby whose heart is not beating. So that would be then it changed, but it didn't come and go, from my recollection, it came, was there, he had a cardiac arrest.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Whilst it was there, was it consistent in appearance or did the appearance alter?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't remember the exact -- at this point in time I'm busy trying to save his life, so I wasn't paying close attention to that pattern, but it was unusual enough for me to take note of it and document it.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You replied a moment ago that a baby going through a deterioration like this would inevitably change colour. But is the event that you're describing different to that process?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: How?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The patches -- I could only really show it in photos.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The way that a dead or dying person looks is their colour will drain, they will initially go a very dusky purple and white. This was patches that didn't fit with -- you tend to go purple and white, it tends to be your arms and legs first, so you become paler at the outside and it tends to then be more purple towards the middle. This had bright red patches, which doesn't fit because red patches means you've got blood going round your body. It had purple patches, it had white patches, and there was no pattern that would fit with what I would expect. And unfortunately, I've seen lots of babies and children who have had the pattern that fits with death or dying and I've not seen these. So if I had photos I could show you the difference, but without that I can't be any clearer, but it was certainly abnormal.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: During your description of these abnormal patches, you've made some hand gestures. Could you tell us where the patches were as best you can recall?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: All over the body.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Does that include the limbs or --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, so the whole body was different patches.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That would be a good moment if you're going to go on to the later part of the note, which I anticipated you would be.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We conventionally, as you may or may not know, break off around 1 o'clock for a lunch break, but you obviously haven't finished your evidence yet, you have to answer more questions and indeed questions on behalf of the defence. Could you be ready, please, doctor, to continue at 2.10? Don't talk to anyone about your evidence between now and then, and indeed, when you've completed your evidence in relation to [Baby A] and you will be leaving us for a period and then coming back again, I will give you another direction that you mustn't talk about anything to do with this case at all to anyone. All right? Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So 2.10 then, please, ladies and gentlemen.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The short adjournment)
(In the absence of the jury)

My Lord, just before the jury come back in (inaudible: distorted) I know we have not been in the practice of having breaks in the afternoon, but the next witness in line, Nurse Bennion, has asked whether an application could be made for screens on her behalf this afternoon. The defence wish to see a statement in advance before the application is made, so I'm asking if we could have a break at the conclusion of this particular witness, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We don't ask to be awkward, because we know that the position is, given where we are, that the likelihood is the application will be granted, but if it is to be dealt with properly --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You want the evidence, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We have to in the position we're in so that's the reason, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Of course and I would want one anyway.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm not just going to rubber stamp it because it has been made.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is not to be difficult; it is just a matter of the correct process.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely right, Mr Myers. It would be wrong of you not to.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Jury in, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)

My Lord, members of the jury, Dr Harkness, if we can just take a step back from your originating notes and go -- Mr Murphy will take us to the summary that we looked at earlier and you questioned the accuracy. If we could go back, please, Mr Murphy, one step.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: In the description of your notes, part of your notes, the third party analyst has recorded as:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Patient arrested win 1 to 2 minutes of starting procedure on other patient."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: When shown that earlier, you raised an eyebrow --
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- and you were right to do so. Let's look at your note. Go down to the bottom of the page.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You have made two entries. The second entry we are now focusing upon is at 21.30 on 8 June, written in retrospect, and herein you're summarising events prior to arrest, I think that word is.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And if we go to the bottom right, where the page stamp has been superimposed on to your notes, I think it reads:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Patient arrest [or arrested] within 1 to 2 minutes of..."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that finishing?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Finishing procedure."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "... on other patient."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's the third baby that you've referred to. Does that accurately --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- reflect the chronology of events?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there then, this procedure on that third baby, how long would that have -- how long did it take?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I can only go off of what -- the timings from the notes, really. Like I'd said before, typically you're spending somewhere between 30 minutes and an hour per baby and I would imagine it would have been somewhere in that region, particularly -- I would have had multiple attempts, failed attempts, to try and do it.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So I would have been busy for -- I don't think I stopped between doing the three. I literally went one baby to the next to the next. So for the time I've documented for [Baby A], in between that time and this, which I think is probably between 30 minutes and an hour.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right. That's for the three babies?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that was for this baby and 30 minutes to an hour.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: (Overspeaking).
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think otherwise with twins, I think it would be somewhere -- again, between 30 minutes and an hour per baby which would fit between 5 o'clock and 8.30.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. So it's a protracted procedure?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And you've described it in general terms, what it involves. So for that period when you were focusing your attention on baby 3, were you doing anything else at that time or were you fully immersed in that task?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: (Overspeaking) like I said before as well, I'd scrubbed, so I'm in sterile equipment, so I can't touch anything or move away from where I am. It takes a great deal of concentration to do it. I've got to try and put a tiny, tiny tube, which is about a millimetre wide, through a tube that's slightly bigger than a millimetre wide into a tiny vein of the same size. So it takes a lot of concentration and focus. So when you're doing it, it's very difficult to be distracted by anything and typically you're left to your own devices as well and only interrupted for something that's urgent.

blocks.text: If we go to slide 168, please. We see movements of -- well, at 167, we see Dr Harkness and a minute or two behind we see Dr Wood, who we're focusing upon.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we click behind, there should be a little more information, not much, and that just tells us that Dr Christopher Wood -- at that time, his swipe data suggests entrance from the maternity neonatal entrance doors in:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "From the medical notes at 20.26 hours [Baby A] was noted to be apnoeic according to the monitor and displayed poor respiratory effort. Dr Harkness was nearby and arrived immediately. I was in a different room on the same ward and attended in less than a
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: minute. When I arrived in nursery room 1, I could see Dr Harkness and at least two other members of the nursing staff, but I cannot recall their names. They had already started assessing [Baby A] and when I arrived, they had started to take apart and dismantle the incubator to allow better access to [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Harkness was providing breaths via a neonatal puff. From memory, I believe there were three, or possibly four cots, in nursery room 1. [Baby A]'s cot was situated on the far wall.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Respiratory support was immediately started using the Neopuff device. From the medical records, I note that the long line was pulled back in case this was a cause. Again from the medical records, oxygen saturations were between 70 to 90%, with a heart rate of 90 to 110. The on-call consultant, Dr Jayaram, was called and asked to urgently attend. I recall he arrived very quickly.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As [Baby A]'s oxygen levels began to fall, along with his heart rate, Dr Harkness managed to intubate [Baby A] on the first attempt at 20.27. Following this, [Baby A]'s heart rate dropped even further and chest compressions were commenced immediately. I briefly assisted Dr Harkness with chest compressions whilst the incubator covers were removed to enable better access to [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Chest compressions on a baby of [Baby A]'s size are carrying out using one or two fingers only.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At this point other staff members had arrived to assist and I was probably the least experienced person there in relation to neonatal babies. I took a step back and switched to scribing."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: At slide 184, and you've already seen this, we see his contribution in that regard:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Everything happened very quickly, within minutes, and at 20.28 hours, on 8 June, I took on the role of scribe. All of the timings recorded would have come from a small fob watch that I use, as we are unable to wear a wristwatch and have to be bare from the elbow down. Scribing is an important role whereby a member of staff records all actions and drugs that were given and acts as timekeeper to ensure the correct drugs were administered in a timely fashion with the correct time gap between each administration.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Harkness was instructing what drugs to be drawn up, the dosage to be used, the preparation and availability of the drugs. I also documented the staff present during the
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: resuscitation. Dr Harkness took the lead role until the consultant, Dr Jayaram, arrived.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Harkness gave out clear instructions to the staff present of what to do next. I recall a member of the nursing staff was asked to go and get the family, a standard procedure that is common in these circumstances. It shows the family that we are doing everything we can to save [Baby A] and I recall they arrived very quickly."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: He then sets out all the entries, which we've been through more than once and we have them, so we need not read them out.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I am now at page 93 of your Lordship's bundle. He summarises, Dr Wood, by saying:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Resuscitation attempts carried on for approximately 40 minutes with little improvement to [Baby A]'s condition. Dr Jayaram discussed with the parents the possible outcome and the withdrawal of life support.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I continued to scribe throughout the duration of the resuscitation efforts, which ultimately concluded at 20.58. In total, [Baby A] was administered adrenaline seven times, three fluid boluses and one sodium bicarbonate bolus over this period, with ongoing chest compressions and ventilation breaths.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I cannot remember what member of staff administered what drug. On the medical notes I recorded the following members of staff as being present..."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And he lists them, but we have that information on our data:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At the conclusion of the resuscitation attempts, I left the room to allow the parents and the senior members of staff some privacy and space with the family.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I personally had no involvement with the family. I had no further involvement in the care of [Baby A]. The clinical notes and my entry relating to the scribing during the resuscitation attempt is the only record I would have made to [Baby A]'s medical notes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As a doctor it is only natural that you start to question: is there anything else we could have done?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I was at the end of a long day shift and [Baby A]'s death came as a shock. This was a child that was considered fairly stable with no major concerns. He wasn't flagged at the beginning of the shift, during the handover, as something significant had
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: happened during the previous shift. There were no concerns around [Baby A]."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And that's the end of the relevant parts of Dr Wood's statement.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So Dr Wood was in the second year of his GP training. This was a secondment, so he would be classed as a senior house officer then, would he?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, in effect.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: With no special training?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: This was his special training.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This was part of his special training, but -yes. And hence he was being a scribe and observer, that sort of thing, rather than an active clinician?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Witness statement of LISA WALKER (read)
Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Members of the jury, I'm going to read some statements from some of the nursing staff who tended to the cares of both [Baby A] and [Baby B] who, as you know, were both in the same room for some of the same time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm now going to page 98 of your Lordship's bundle and to the statement of Lisa Walker.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The statement is dated 23 July 2018:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am currently employed at the Countess of Chester Hospital as a neonatal nursery assistant within the neonatal unit. I first started work at the Countess of Chester on ward 50 as a healthcare assistant, then in August 2008 I applied for the role of neonatal nursery assistant."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She sets out the shift patterns. Nights at 19.30 through to 8 in the morning, and a day shift, 7.30 in the morning to 8 pm at night. And she says during the period between 2015 and 2016 she believes she was working full-time hours. She says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The half-hour overlap between shifts allows time to hand over to the next shift coming on duty. It is during this time when you are allocated the babies for whom you will be responsible
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: during your shift. It was the responsibility of that shift leader to allocate who you would be looking after, depending on each individual's skill base and grading along with the requirements of the unit.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The system has been changed some time ago and it is now the responsibility of the shift leader from the previous shift who allocates what nurse or nursery assistant is looking after what baby or babies.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As a nursery assistant we can sometimes have up to four babies depending on how busy the unit is. During the handover you're provided with a brief summary for each baby and their medical needs. As a nursery assistant I have quite a lot" --
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry to be pedantic, but it's "medical history", it says.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During the handover you are provided with a brief summary for each baby and their medical history.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As a nursery assistant, I have quite a lot of responsibility. We maintain and establish feeding regimes. Some babies may be on a nasal prong oxygen, which I will be responsible for monitoring and will carry out work as directed by the trained staff."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She then applied her mind to [Baby A] and [Baby B]:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have had the opportunity to review the nursing notes of the twins, [Baby A] and [Baby B], to refresh my memory and assist with this interview.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "From the notes, I was aware of when they were born and the fact they both went straight to nursery 1, the intensive care unit of the neonatal unit."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As a nursing assistant I am not qualified to work with the babies in nursery room 1. This would be left for the band 5 and 6 nurses. As a neonatal nursery nurse I predominantly work within nursery rooms 3 and 4 in the special care baby unit. As the babies progress and become stronger, their needs become less and they require less monitoring. This is when the babies will be moved into room 2, then on to rooms 3 and 4, where they will be discharged from hospital to go home. We commonly refer to rooms 3 and 4 as the growing and feeding rooms.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 8 June 2015 I can confirm that I was working the first one of three night shifts, starting on the 8th at 19.30 hours to 08.00 in the morning the next day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I then worked the following two night shifts on the 9th and 10 June.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In relation to 8 June 2015 I was aware that baby [Baby A] suffered a collapse and sadly died. From the notes, the incident was around 20.26, I can confirm that I was working a night shift on that particular day but I had no involvement with the incident at 20.26 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I had no direct dealings whatsoever in the care of [Baby A] and [Baby B] during the three night shifts I carried out on 8, 9 and 10 June."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She lists all the people who were present, which we can show through other means.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She recalls being made aware that [Baby A] had suddenly collapsed on the night shift, but she states she was on duty in nursery rooms 3 and 4, caring for other babies at the time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She does remember one member of staff involved in the incident asking someone to go and get the parents. She couldn't remember who went to get the parents but she says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I don't think it was me, but I cannot be 100% certain."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She confirms again that she had no involvement in the collapse of [Baby A]. She says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "It is not unusual to be unaware of other incidents occurring on the unit when you are focusing on treating and caring for the babies that you are responsible for.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I recall that the unit was particularly busy around this time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Some time during the shift I was made aware that [Baby A] had sadly died. I do not remember who or how I was informed but I do recall the sadness in the atmosphere that passed through the unit. It's always sad to be informed that one of the babies in the unit had died and I do recall around this period of time there appeared to be an increase.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have worked on the unit for the past 10 years and prior to this period of time I have only experienced a couple of baby deaths on the unit. At the time I remember coming into work to be informed that another baby had died. It was a very sad time on the unit and I remember thinking, what on earth is happening?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The following night shift, on 9 June 2015, I came to work alongside Cheryl Cuthbertson-Taylor in nursery rooms 3 and 4. I don't remember the exact time. It was the handover and the day staff had left the unit. I was made aware that an assistance call for [Baby B], [Baby A]'s twin sister, had been put out. I don't remember what member of staff asked but I was asked to go and get the family.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I think I went up to the parents' room and informed the midwife who was dealing with [Mother of Babies A & B], [Baby B]'s mum.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Once the family arrived on the unit I left them with the nursing staff in the intensive care unit, nursery room 1. It is common practice that all the trained staff and nurses would remain on the unit assisting with the emergency and the nursery staff would be there to support in any way they can. It could be that we take over the care of all the other babies in nursery rooms 2, 3 and 4, managing their feeds, et cetera.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I had no further dealings with the family on that evening. They remained in nursery room 1 and another member of staff would have supported them. I do remember the [Surname of Babies A & B] family as I cared for [Baby B] on several occasions when she was moved into nursery rooms 3 and 4 in preparation of going home.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This would have been several weeks later when [Baby B] was stronger and she had moved out of the intensive care unit and into the special care baby rooms.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember having a lot of interaction with [Mother of Babies A & B], [Baby B]'s mum, and the family some weeks later, talking about them and trying to support and reassure them.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I remember a conversation with [Mother of Babies A & B] when she questioned the reason for [Baby A]'s death, wondering if her blood condition was to blame. She asked to speak with a consultant to try and understand what happened.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't know if she had those conversations with anybody."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And Lisa Walker does not have any other relevant information with which she could assist.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of LAURA EAGLES (read)

The next statement is made by Laura Eagles, dated 25 July 2018, stating that she at that point in time was employed at the Countess of Chester Hospital as a band 6 senior neonatal practitioner, having worked in the hospital since 2003:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have been asked regarding my knowledge of babies [Baby A] and [Baby B] and in particular the shifts of the 8th, 9th and 10 June 2015. I have had the opportunity to read through the clinical nursing notes to assist with this statement.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I can confirm that I was working a long day shift on the unit during 8 June 2015 from 07.30 hours to 20.00 hours. I was off duty on 9 June and returned to a long day again on the 10th.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I believe that I was in charge as shift leader on 8 June 2015. I have looked at the off-duty sheets for this period and the allocated team leader/shift leader would normally appear in blue. Unfortunately, the unit only has a photocopy of this paperwork now. However, my name has been circled for that day, which is another indication I was shift leader for that particular day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "With regards to 8 June 2015 I have been made aware that baby [Baby A] suffered a collapse at 20.26 hours and sadly died. Then on 10 June, baby [Baby B] also suffered a collapse at 00.30 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was not involved with either of the two mentioned incidents. I have no recollection of any dealings with [Baby A]'s resus. I had no direct involvement in his care during the day shift of 8 June.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 10 June 2015 I came into work for a long day shift. I was allocated to be the designated nurse for baby [Baby B]. I received a handover at 07.30 hours from [Nurse A], who had been on night duty with [Baby B]. I don't recall the handover. It is only from the nursing records I am able to say it was [Nurse A] who handed over to me. I would have been made aware that [Baby A] had passed away. I don't remember who informed me or exactly when.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During the handover [Nurse A] would have discussed with me the sudden collapse [Baby B] had around 00.30 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: A blood sample was taken and tested for clotting. I am aware that another blood sample was taken from [Baby B], which was sent for testing due to the blood disorder mum had.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "There were some concerns [Baby B] may have some form of clotting disorder. The blood samples were to try and establish if the blood condition had anything to do with his sudden collapse and the purple blotches that appeared. The results from the blood samples are received some weeks later and generally dealt with as an outpatient. The nursing staff do not know the results.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When I took over from [Nurse A] at 08.00 hours on 10 June 2015, [Baby B] was ventilated. She was on normal TPN [total parenteral nutrition] and lipids. She was on morphine and she was on small amounts of feeds. She was stable throughout the day and the only incident of note was at 19.25 hours that evening when I documented that [Baby B] had a blocked tube.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The alarms on the monitors had activated.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I remember the incident because all the doctors at the time were in theatre. I can't be sure but I think they were in theatre for the delivery of twins.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I informed Chris Booth, who was shift leader. He came to assist me with supporting [Baby B]'s breathing.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I asked another member of staff to go into theatre to inform one of the doctors that [Baby B]'s tube was blocked. I don't know who that was. I can't remember.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Chris and I removed the blocked tube, which is normal practice. We maintained [Baby B]'s airway and assisted her with her breathing, using Neopuff.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Brunton, one of the consultants, came out of theatre and on to the unit. He checked if we were okay.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I remember him asking if she was breathing, which [Baby B] was. Her sats readings were good and she was pink. He said, keep her like that until we come through. He then went on to suggest seeing if any other consultants were in the office who were not on call.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby B] wasn't re-intubated, she was breathing for herself and she was put on to CPAP. She was checked over and she continued to breathe for herself. I think I handed [Baby B] back over to [Nurse A], who was on night duty again.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby B] remained on the unit for some time until she was ready to be discharged to go home. I do not have any other relevant information in relation to [Baby A] or [Baby B] [she states]."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of ELIZABETH MARSHALL (read)
Next, a statement from one Elizabeth Marshall, dated 8 April 2019, stating:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am a band 4 neonatal assistant within the neonatal unit of the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I have been asked by Cheshire Police to provide details of my shift on 8 June 2015 and any involvement of care that I may have provided to [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On this shift I was working on a night shift. My shift will have started at 19.30 on the 8th and finished at 8 am on 9 June 2015. When I came on duty I would have been informed what nursery I was working in and what babies I was caring for. I would have been given a briefing about that baby from a member of the day shift. I cannot recall any personal memories of this shift."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She reviews the rotas, names who was on duty with her. She says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Upon reviewing the files I have noted there were 15 babies in total on the unit to be cared for on this shift. As this was a busy shift I may have been allocated to care for more than one baby. I was allocated to work in either nursery 2, 3 or 4. The notes say I looked after a baby whose initials are TB.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I have been unable to access the notes to review any of the other babies I may have looked after. I have no memory to assist.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "It is very rare that I would ever work in nursery 1 where [Baby A] was. I did not have any involvement in [Baby A]'s care. I was working for the whole night in other nurseries. The unit is very small and on occasions you are aware of things going on in other nurseries."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: But she cannot recall any details of that shift other than the fact that she became aware that [Baby A] passed away.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of MINNA LAPPALAINEN (read)
Nurse Minna Lappalainen made a statement dated 28 March 2018, stating:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have been asked to comment on baby [Baby A] and in particular his care on 8 June 2015."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She could not say with certainty whether she was working on 8 June 2015, but confirms that she was working a day shift on 9 June 2015, when she was allocated the task of completing the bereavement paperwork in relation to [Baby A] who'd passed away during the night. By the time she started her shift, the other staff were no longer on duty and the parents had left the unit.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She was given a handover by Mel Taylor and Lucy Letby, who had been on nights, and completing the bereavement procedure during the night. She can't remember any specifics:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Mel and Lucy did not remain on duty with me to complete the bereavement pack. To be involved in such an incident involving the death of a patient is emotionally and physically draining. I cannot recall the mental or physical state of Mel or Lucy.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The bereavement procedure and paperwork is a large folder, which includes lots of forms to complete with people and agencies that need to be contacted and informed of the death, which includes the coroner.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: It is designed so nothing is missed or overlooked."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She cannot recall exactly what she completed in the bereavement pack, but she would have signed next to all her actions.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of JOANNE WILLIAMS (read)

Joanne Williams, another nurse within the unit, made a statement on 3 October 2018 stating that she is a band, or was at that point, band 6 neonatal practitioner within the unit. She stated that she'd had the opportunity to read through the clinical and nursing notes and confirmed that she wasn't working on the 7th or 8 June 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She was working a day shift on 9 June and on the 10th and 11 June. She explains the process of the huddle, which we've heard more than once now, and unless otherwise ask to do so, I won't repeat. Then she sets out the staffing levels. She says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "One member of staff to each baby in the ICU. One member of staff to two babies in the high dependency unit. One member of staff to four babies in the special care unit. These are guidelines set out by BAPM, the British Association of Perinatal Medicine.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Once allocated a baby or babies, the staff member will go to the cot side and have a verbal handover with the designated nurse currently looking after that baby.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: At the end of each cot are the charts for each baby.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The charts detail everything that happens with that baby, including fluids, feeds, nappy changes, observations, blood gas charts, apnoea/bradycardia/desaturations, and pain charts.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Anyone who has anything to do with that individual baby should endorse the charts.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The nursing notes are computerised and can be written up at the time or retrospectively at the end of the shift and normally
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: completed by the designated nurse or anyone who's had any direct involvement with that baby or child.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was a designated nurse for [Baby B] during the day shift of 9 June 2015. I can't recall who I took over from. How far, I do recall handing over to [Nurse A], who was on night duty. My shift that day began at 7.30 am and finished at 8 pm and I believe [Baby B] was the only baby I was designated to look after.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: As [Baby B] was in nursery room 1, the ICU/intensive care unit, it is unlikely I would have had any other babies to look after but I cannot say for sure.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The shift leader, on allocating what baby was to be looked after by what member of staff, would have been very mindful and sensitive to the sad loss of [Baby A], [Baby B]'s sibling, the previous evening. I actually cannot remember who was the shift leader that day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby B] remained in the ICU/nursery room 1. Her cot was situated to the right of the door. I don't recall how many babies were on the unit at that time. The shift doesn't stand out in my memory as one that was unusually busy, although we were always busy at that time. I remember that we had the room screens or dividers up to give the family some privacy following the loss of their son the night before.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The family remained at [Baby B]'s cot side the entire day. The only time the parents left the unit was for mum, [Mother of Babies A & B], to get some rest or something to eat, and she would only leave if the grandparents were present.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This was completely understandable with the sudden and unexpected death of [Baby A] the previous evening on 9 June 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "My main aim throughout the shift was to keep things calm and quiet for the family. I assisted mum twice during the day with skin-to-skin contact and taking lots of photos of [Baby B] while she was out of the incubator.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby B] got a little bit tired, so I placed her back on CPAP to assist.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "All of the entries made on the medical or nursing notes are made retrospectively and generally completed towards the end of the shift. The computer system timestamps each entry.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Throughout the entire shift nothing significant happened. [Baby B] was stable. She was progressing well.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She had two periods out of the incubator and off CPAP with skinto-skin contact with mum. During the time out of the incubator, [Baby B] was breathing for herself. Due to the sad events of the previous evening, [Baby A]'s death, I tried to keep the atmosphere relaxed and calm for the family. Most of the day we had the screen up for the family, providing them with some privacy.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I cannot recall if there was another family in the nursery room, nursery room 1, during this shift.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Nothing stands out.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Although I had no direct dealing with [Baby A], his death came as an unexpected shock to the unit.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Throughout the shift [Baby B] was progressing well. There was a slight increase in her breathing at one point and she was placed back on CPAP. I put this down to her getting a little tired after being out of the incubator.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Taking into consideration her size, gestation and antenatal prognosis, she was doing relatively well. She was small and you can never become complacent with neonatal babies. However, there were no obvious signs or events during my shift with [Baby B] on 9 June 2015 that caused me any concern when I went off duty that night.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I do remember noticing the following morning that [Baby B] had been re-ventilated during the night shift, which came as a bit of a shock as she was doing so well.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Nothing really surprises me with neonatal babies anymore as they can deteriorate quickly.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby B] remained on the unit and progressed well, eventually going home some weeks later."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of [Mother of non-indictment baby] (read)
[Mother of non-indictment baby] made a statement on 22 December 2021.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She was the mother of a baby in the unit at the time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She states that she was in the unit on 8 June 2015. She intended to visit the unit but was prevented from doing so because there was an emergency on the unit:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At around [this is page 117, my Lord] 19.00 hours a nurse called [Nurse A] came up to my room to let me know that [her] baby was okay and reassured her that [her] baby was doing fine. [Her] baby was sharing a room with twins [Baby B] and [Baby A], who were born the day before on 7 June."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So her child is the third baby that Dr Harkness made reference to.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The following day on Tuesday 9 June, this witness and her husband went to the unit. She had learned that, sadly, one of the twins had died. She entered nursery 1, she could see screens had been put up that actually divided the room into two halves. Her baby's incubator was positioned to the left side of that room, which is the side nearest to the reception, and the twins would have been to the right side:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I could not see the right side of the room as they were trying to keep the other half private."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She would describe the screen as a large type of curtain made of coloured fabric on wheels. The curtain was about 2 feet away from the ceiling, so even when standing, we couldn't see over the top. The curtain hung about 10 inches from the floor, the fabric of the curtain was thick, couldn't see through it or make out shadows or anything on the other side. The curtain was pulled across in such a way that there were no gaps on either side. There were two doors that lead into the ICU. You could walk through the door to the left side where [her] baby's incubator was positioned. The second door was towards the right side of the position and closest to where the twins had been:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The screens were up for a couple of days.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I remember the twins' parents, [Mother of Babies A & B] and [Father of Babies A & B], having other relatives visit them. Initially we'd see them outside the nursery but then they would go behind the screens. She and her husband went in the room with he baby on the opposite side."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She says the screens were definitely up for 2 or 3 days but she's unsure whether they were still present on 11 June when her baby was moved to nursery 2.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: May I just say something to members of the media in relation to that witness who's been named in court. There is no power under the law to prohibit the publication of the name of that witness, which would lead to the identification or may lead to the identification of the baby in question, but I would just ask that if any of that part of the evidence is reported that sensitivity is taken in relation to that and
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: simply saying the mother perhaps of the third baby in that nursery, nursery room 1, where the twins were could be used rather than leading to identification.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: As I say, I can't do anything by law, but I do ask for some sensitivity in relation to that on behalf of people involved. It has no relevance. That evidence has no relevance to the babies who are the subject of the counts on the indictment.
